title: Screening and regulation of nanozyme activity via liquid metals coined electron rearrangement and phase engineering

paper_content.abstract: Liquid metals (LMs) have been used for design of advanced materials by leveraging their unique liquid and electronic properties. Here, we design a series of liquid metal-buffered amorphous molybdenum sulfide nanozymes with different gallium indium ratios, in which Ga In MoS 75.5 24.5 X nanozymes exhibit the enzyme-like activity, superior to the crystalline MoS . This has been verified and assigned to the roles of liquid metal: (i) serving as the building template, (ii) phase engineering with catalytic active sites, (iii) electron-rich microenvironment for improving catalytic activity. Besides, the amorphous Ga In MoS nanozyme possesses oxidase (OXD)-like and 75.5 24.5 X S nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide oxidase (NOX)-like activiSty to achieve multiple-enzyme-like E cascade catalytic reactions, disrupting intratumoral redox and metabolism homeostasis. As the R example of leveraging liquid metal as a well-desiPgned platform to screen high-performance N nanozyme with excellent therapeutic effects, thNis work highlights the roles of tailored electronic I structure and phase engineering for regula tion of catalytic activity of nanozymes and may also E broaden the application of liquid metaLl in catalysis and biomedical field.
paper_content.introduction:
Liquid metals (LMs) aAre enigmatic materials, with simultaneous metallic and liquid nature.1, 2 The most striking features of liquid metals are the amorphous property and unusual electronic microenvironment, which originate from the electron-rich metallic cores and free delocalized electron clouds.3, 4 Such characters make liquid metals show great potential to tune the physical, chemical, and electronic properties of materials for boosting their performance in various engineering applications.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 More importantly, liquid metals represent a promising technical route for manufacturing modular advanced materials.3, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 The obtained combinatorial materials can readily maintain the typical characteristics of liquid metals and may attain better functionality.20 In particular, the intrinsic amorphous nature of liquid metals creates a facile pathway for phase engineering of materials, thus deriving more intriguing properties and innovative applications.21, 22 Interestingly, liquid metals have also shown promising prospects in catalysis by capitalizing on their unique electronic properties.23, 24, 25, 26 For example, recent studies have reported that liquid metals could create dynamic uniform catalytic sites and favorable electronic structures for catalytic metal species to remarkably enhance their catalytic capability.27, 28, 29 Similarly, liquid metals have been proposed as a unique electron mediator for temporary electron storage, and promoted the extraction and transfer of electrons, as well as charge separation, greatly improving the optoelectronic property of perovskite films.30 Furthermore, the representative Ga-based liquid metal alloys with excellent biocompatibility and attractive flexibility, have recently aroused great interest in the biological field including cancer therapy, antimicrobial treatment, and bioimaging.31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, S39, 40, 41, 42, 43 These studies indicate the exceptional advantages of liquid metals to create advanced materials for catalytic and biomedicine applications.

Nanozymes are nanomaterials with inherent Nenzyme-mimicking catalytic properties, and have ignited increasing attention due to their adv antages of high catalytic stability and durability, easy preparation, and low cost.44, 45, 46, 47 ALlthough promising, the unsatisfactory catalytic efficiency of nanozymes remains a crucial issue for future practical applications.48, 49, 50, 51, 52 This demonstrates the vital necessity of developing an appropriate strategy to optimize the nanozyme catalytic performance. From aAn in-depth perspective, the catalytic active sites and local electronic characteristics determine their catalytic performance to a large extent.49, 50, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57 Notably, phase engineering of nanomaterials has demonstrated remarkable prospects in the catalysis field because this process modulates the atomic arrangements and electronic structure of catalysts, hence providing unusual catalytic activity.58, 59 Especially, amorphous materials possess distinctive disordered atomic arrangement that enables them with abundant active sites and optimized electronic configurations, which are beneficial for enhancing their catalytic properties.60, 61 Thus, combining the ability of phase engineering and the unique electronic properties, liquid metals are expected to be a dream matrix to construct high-performance nanozymes. However, the potential of liquid metal in regulating nanozyme catalytic activity has rarely been explored mechanistically. In particular, previous research efforts have focused on the application of liquid metal-based nanozyme while overlooking the catalytic potential of liquid metals for screening and regulation of nanozyme activity. 62, 63

Here we design and screen the liquid metals-buffered nanozymes, in which the liquid metals can not only initiate phase engineering to generate an amorphous nanozyme with abundant catalytic active sites, but also afford an electron-rich microenvironment to optimize the electronic structure of nanozymes for improving the catalytic performance (Fig. 1). We first prepare a series of molybdenum sulfide nanozymes by using five liquid metals with the composition of Ga In 1-x x (with x=0, 0.125, 0.245, 0.375, and 0.50) as templates, and these nanozymes feature uniformly core-shell structure and amorphous property. We observe that tShese nanozymes exhibit peroxidase (POD)-like activities, in which the LM MoS nanozymes (LM=Ga In ) present the best X R 75.5 24.5 catalytic activity. Then, the role of liquid metals inP regulating the enzyme-mimicking catalytic activity of LM MoS nanozymes is explored. WNe demonstrate that, compared to crystalline MoS , X 2 the amorphous LM MoS X nanozymes expo se abundant active sites and defects, and show about a 10-fold increase in the POD-like catalLytic activity, together with a significantly higher glutathione (GSH) consumption ability. Meanwhile, this strategy can turn on the oxidase (OXD)-like and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide oxidase (NOX)-like activities of LM MoS to achieve cascade X catalytic reactions, eveAntually leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrate that the LM MoS nanozymes with multienzyme-mimicking X catalytic activity can trigger a highly efficient cascade reaction to disrupt intratumoral redox and metabolic homeostasis, eventually killing tumor cells. In this work, we introduce liquid metal with advantages in synthesis and catalysis to screen and regulate the catalytic and therapeutic effects of nanozymes for efficient tumor inhibition. Our work not only investigates the catalytic activity of liquid metal-buffered nanozyme with different gallium indium ratios, but also elucidates the mechanism underlying the enhanced enzyme-like catalytic activity through density functional theory (DFT) calculations. This study offers promising insights into the design and regulation of nanozymes, with potential benefits for future biomedical applications of liquid metals.

The design and preparation of liquid metal-buffered nanozymes
As shown in Fig. 1a, the nanozyme was synthesized through facile probe sonication. Liquid metals with different ratios of gallium and indium were prepared by dissolving a calculated amount of In pellets in liquid Ga. The resultant liquid metal alloys should retain their liquid states at close to room temperature to ensure the subsequent liquid-liquid interfacial reactions.64 According to the previous reports, the molar fraction of In should below 50 at% in order to ensure their liquid states at close to room temperature.65, 66 Specifically, the composition of Ga In (with x = 0, 0.125, 0.245, S1-x x 0.375, and 0.50) were chosen and prepared to design a series oSf liquid metal-buffered nanozymes. Molybdenum is a low-cost and biocompatible transition metal with multiple oxidation states, which endows Mo-based nanomaterials with tunablPe enzyme-like activity.67 Among Mo-based nanomaterials, molybdenum sulfide features unNique structural and electronic properties and show superior performance in various applica tions, especially for catalysis.68, 69 The generated nanozymes were denoted as Ga 50 In 5L0 MoS X , Ga 62.5 In 37.5 MoS X , Ga 75.5 In 24.5 MoS X , Ga 87.5 In 12.5 MoS , Ga MoS . During this procedure, liquid metal served as a template to trigger in situ X 100 X galvanic replacement reactions between liquid metal droplets and MoS 2- ions to produce core– 4 shell nanostructures uApon ultrasonication. The thermodynamic driving force underlying the galvanic replacement reaction originates from the difference in redox potentials between the two metal-based species.21, 64 The size distribution of nanoparticles became narrower with higher sonication intensity applied (Supplementary Fig. 1). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images illustrated the well-constructed core-shell structures of the synthesized five nanozymes (Fig. 2a). Then, the energy dispersive spectroscopic (EDS) mapping and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results demonstrated the existence of Ga, In, Mo and S elements in these nanozymes (Supplementary Fig. 2-3). Next, high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) images indicated the amorphous nature of five nanozymes (Fig. 2a). According to previous studies, the intrinsic amorphous nature of liquid metals and short reaction time are considered the main reasons for the formation of the amorphous structure.4, 11 Dynamic light scattering (DLS) results of five nanozymes revealed that their hydrodynamic diameters were mainly distributed around 300 nm (Fig. 2b). The surface zeta potential measurement showed that these nanozymes were negatively charged (Fig. 2c). Then, we explored the POD-like activity of five nanozymes by monitoring the oxidation of 2, 2'-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS) at 415 nm. As revealed in Fig. 2d and 2e, obvious ABTS oxidation could be detected, indicating that all five nanozymes possessed POD-like activity. Among them, Ga In MoS exhibited the highest 75.5 24.5 X catalytic activity, while Ga In MoS showed a relatively low activity. According to previous 50 50 X studies, the Indium content in GaIn alloys significantly affects the disordered structure and the charge density distribution of alloys, thus influencing their aSmorphous structure and electrical conductivity.70 Specifically, the alloying of Ga with In causes more disordered structure. This amorphous structure is beneficial for the high catalPytic performance of catalysts. However, the electrical conductivity of GaIn alloys decreasesN with In alloying of Ga because the charge density I near the In atoms is significantly smaller, which is unfavorable to the electron transfer and the E subsequent catalytic process of catalyLsts. Thus, the catalytic activity of the resulting nanozymes C could show a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing with increasing In content in the I T GaIn alloy. These findings could explain the experimental results that the alloying effect of In with R Ga favored the catalyAtic reaction, while lower or higher In contents compromised the catalytic activity. We further employed XPS spectra to characterize the electronic properties of these nanozymes. As displayed in Fig. 2f, the binding energies of Mo 3d were positively shifted in Ga In MoS and Ga MoS nanozymes, in comparison to other nanozymes, revealing the 75.5 24.5 X 100 X occurrence of electron transfer and rearrangement. Moreover, we have analyzed the surface valence states of Ga In MoS and Ga MoS , revealing their different Mo oxidation states 75.5 24.5 X 100 X (Supplementary Fig. 4). This meant that liquid metals with varying compositions had different effects on the electronic properties and valence states of the resulting nanozyme.

DFT Calculations
To gain insights into the reasons for the enhanced enzyme-like catalytic activity of liquid metal- buffered nanozyme, density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on first principles were conducted to investigate their electronic structures. First, three computational surface models representing ideal MoS , MoS (amorphization) and LM MoS were constructed to elucidate their 2 X X microscopic electron structures. As shown in the charge density maps (Fig. 5a), the amorphous MoS exhibited an increased electron density around Mo atoms compared with the MoS model. x 2 Notably, the LM MoS model achieved the highest electron density, indicating the electron X donation from liquid metal to Mo atoms. Moreover, the differential charge density of LM MoS X in Fig. 5b revealed the electron donation from the liquid metal to Mo atoms. In addition, the Bader charge of Mo in MoS , MoS , and LM MoS was calculated. The Bader charge analysis indicated 2 X X a charge gain of 0.52 e- on the Mo sites in the MoS relative to MoS . Compared to MoS , the X 2 X electron accumulation on the Mo sites increased by an additional 0.21 e- in the LM MoS , which X further confirmed that electron donation from liquid metal to Mo atoms. Then, the density of states (DOS) of MoS , MoS and LM MoS models, as shown in Fig. 5c, revealed that LM MoS 2 X X S X exhibited a significantly higher DOS near the Fermi level and sSeveral new hybrid electronic states E appeared compared to MoS and MoS , indicating stronger interaction and charge transfer 2 X R between LM MoS and adsorbates.51, 74 FurthermorPe, the d-band center of the Mo orbital was X calculated based on the DOS of MoS , MoS Nand LM MoS . As shown in Fig. 5d, LM MoS 2 X X X I nanozymes exhibited an upward shift in d band center position (-1.686 eV), which was E significantly nearer to the Fermi levelL than those of MoS 2 (-3.619 eV) and MoS X (-2.908 eV). The C state near to the Fermi level contributed to the interaction between the adsorbed substrate and LM I T MoS nanozyme, thereby favoring the catalytic reaction.56 These results were consistent with the X R kinetic parameters stuAdy (Supplementary Table 2), in which the reduced K m value indicated that A the LM MoS had a higher affinity to H O . Based on these results, we confirmed that the pivotal X 2 2 role of liquid metal, i.e., amorphization, and electron transfer, endowing LM MoS nanozymes X with optimized enzyme-like catalytic activity. In our designed system, on the one hand, liquid metals ingeniously endowed the nanozymes with amorphous property, thus providing abundant active sites for catalysis. On the other hand, the liquid metals matrix and the amorphous character of nanozymes led to a favorable electronic perturbation, which could promote electron transfer and optimize the reaction process, thereby boosting the catalytic behavior. These data indicated the superiority of liquid metal for the construction of high-performance nanozyme.

In summary, we leverage liquid metal as a well-designed platform to screen high-performance nanozyme with excellent therapeutic effects. First, we have designed and synthesized a series of liquid metal-buffered nanozymes and screened the most favorable nanozyme to achieve efficient tumor catalytic therapy. In this strategy, the liquid metals possess inherent unique advantages: (i) serving as the building template of nanozymes, (ii) initiatingS phase engineering to generate an E amorphous nanozyme with abundant catalytic active sites, (iii) featuring electron-rich R microenvironment to affect electronic structure of naPnozymes, which are beneficial for regulating nanozyme catalytic activity. The amorphous LMN MoS nanozymes exhibit superior multienzyme- X I mimicking cascade catalytic activity, whic h can induce ROS burst and metabolic imbalance to E drive the efficient catalytic therapy Lof tumors with great biocompatibility. reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript reports the design of LM-buffered amorphous MoSx nanozymes using Ga-In alloys as templates. The
authors synthesize a series of Ga1-x Inx MoSx nanozymes and identify Ga75.5 In24.5 MoSx as exhibiting superior POD-like
activity compared to crystalline MoS2. They attribute this enhancement to LM’s roles in templating, inducing amorphization,
and providing an electron-rich microenvironment. The optimized nanozyme demonstrates multi-enzyme activities (POD-,
OXD-, and NOX-like), enabling cascade reactions that disrupt redox/metabolic homeostasis in tumor cells. In vitro and in
vivo studies show efficient ROS generation, GSH/NADH depletion, mitochondrial damage, and tumor growth inhibition. DFT
calculations suggest electron transfer from LM optimizes the electronic structure for catalysis. The work applies established
methodologies without demonstrating a significant conceptual or practical leap beyond existing literature. The absence of
comparative analysis with relevant systems and recurring presentation issues further diminishes its suitability for Nature
Communications. Should the authors address these gaps (e.g., by rigorously benchmarking against competitors and
clarifying the innovation boundary), this study may find a better fit in a specialized journal. Therefore, I recommend rejection
in its current form.
Major Weaknesses Reinforcing Rejection:
1. Combines two well-explored materials (LM + MoS2) without novel design principles or mechanistic insights. The concept
of using LM (Ga-In alloys) for catalysis is well-established (e.g., Refs 23–30, 62–63), as is MoS2-based nanozyme design
(Ref 55). The work combines these existing strategies without introducing a transformative mechanism, material, or
application.
2. Claims of LM’s unique roles lack substantial evidence, except for citing prior literatures
3. Catalytic performance lacks comparison to state-of-the-art LM-based catalysts or high-activity MoS2-based nanozymes.
Assertions of "superior activity" remain unsupported without context.
4. No optimization data for critical parameters (e.g., sonication power/temperature effects).
Other concerns:
1. Explain POD, ABTS, ……
2. Do not use “liquid metal” and “LM” casually.
3. In Fig. 2D, what is the meaning of the curve named control?
4. “Among them, Ga75.5In24.5 MoSX presented the highest catalytic activity”. Why? The explanation below is insufficient.
5. The LM MoSx model in Fig. 5 is too coarse. MoSx is an amorphous structure and the LM is wrapped by it, as shown in
Fig. 2, which is almost irrelevant with the model in Fig. 5.
6. “the amorphous MoSx exhibited an increased electron the amorphous exhibited an increased electron”, but I can only see
an opposite trend. Also, “revealing the electron donation from LM to Mo atoms” is questionable.
7. What’s the meaning of “d-band center” and what’s the algorithm to determine its center?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, Zhang et al. designed a series of liquid metal-buffered nanozymes and screened the most favorable
nanozyme to achieve efficient tumor catalytic therapy. The findings highlight the roles of tailored electronic structure and
phase engineering for regulating the catalytic activity of nanozymes. Authors demonstrate that this is the first report of
screening and regulating the catalytic and therapeutic effects of LM nanozymes to achieve efficient tumor therapy. The
overall work is well-designed, and the application of LM in catalysis and the biomedical field is interesting. However, at the
current stage, the characterization of the structure-activity relationship and the anti-cancer mechanism of LM-based
nanozyme is not solid. Also, other issues need to be addressed.
1)The most significant concern of utilizing LM-based nanozymes for catalytic cancer therapy lies in the intrinsic property of
LM. As is known, amorphous LM nanoparticles could gradually transform into crystalline material, especially in aqueous
solution. Due to such a dynamic process, the composition of LM-based nanozyme could hardly be maintained during in vitro
and in vivo experiments or characterizations. Also, it is necessary to ensure that the MoSx content in a series of LM-buffered
nanozymes is the same. Or else, the differences in nanozyme activity could also be influenced by different MoSx contents.
2)In a recently published paper (Small 2025, 2502752), FeOx was used to hybridize LM to generate nanozymes. Therefore,
the reason for choosing molybdenum sulfide should be clarified to distinguish the innovation of this work from previous
works, and the advantages of molybdenum sulfide should be explained as well.
3)It was demonstrated that Ga75.5In24.5 (commercial Gallium-Indium eutectic) MoSX performed the best catalytic activity,
but the possible reason was not given. With subtle variations of the compositions, the melting points and the fluidities of
resultant LM-MoSX nanozymes would alter significantly. In this context, the discussion of the catalytic activity of LM-MoSX
nanozymes should be careful. Additionally, the authors did not provide detailed synthesis methods and characterization
techniques. It is suggested to supplement relevant details.
4)Although decorating with HA, it remains challenging for LM-MoSX nanozyme (ca. 300 nm) to achieve efficient cellular
uptake and high accumulation in the stiff 4T1 tumor via intravenous injection (Figure S35). And what is the half-life of LM-
MoSX nanozyme?
5)In Figure S2B, D, the In 3d curves were poorly fitted.
6)In Figure S20, the curve shape of EPR result of O2•− seems abnormal. Please confirm the result and the discussion.
7)In Figure S27, why did the cellular fluorescence of DAPI present large deviations at variable time points?
8)The changes in particle size and potential of LM MoSx should be measured after the modification of HA.
9)In Figure S33, there is a difference in H&E staining of the lung between the H-LM MoSx group and the control group. Were
the images captured at the same magnification?
10)In Figure S35, quantitative data on in vivo biodistribution should be supplemented.
11)The stability test of the LM MoSx nanozymes should be provided.
12)In the article, POD-like activity was used to screen for suitable ratios of GaIn. Why not use other nanozyme activities for
screening?
13)In Figure 6J, the live and dead cells co-staining was not well performed, and the cell morphology could hardly be
distinguished.Please provide fluorescence images under high magnification.
14)The grammar and language of the manuscript should be carefully polished.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors present a comprehensive and well-executed study on liquid metal-buffered MoSₓ nanozymes, systematically
synthesized using Ga–In alloys to optimize catalytic performance. The Ga₇₅.₅In₂₄.₅-based nanozyme exhibits enhanced
peroxidase-, oxidase-, and NADH oxidase-like activities, enabling a catalytic cascade that disrupts redox homeostasis in
cancer cells and induces selective cytotoxicity both in vitro and in vivo. The combination of multi-enzyme functionality,
effective tumor targeting, and minimal toxicity underscores the therapeutic potential of this platform. The study’s originality
lies in leveraging liquid metal templating to precisely control nanozyme composition, structure, and electronic properties,
representing a clear advancement over previous LM-based nanozyme approaches. The conclusions are well-supported by
comprehensive materials characterization, catalytic assays, theoretical modeling, and biological validation. The
experimental methodology is appropriate and rigorously executed. Overall, this work constitutes a significant contribution to
nanozyme research and catalytic cancer therapy.
To further enhance the manuscript, several clarifications and suggestions are
proposed as detailed in the following comments (also provided in the attached file).
1. Particle Size and Delivery: A potential concern is the relatively large hydrodynamic size of the nanozyme (~300 nm
diameter). Particles of this size may have limited tumor penetration and faster clearance by the mononuclear
phagocyte system. The in vivo success after HA coating suggests good tumor accumulation capability, but the authors might comment
on how the size could influence distribution. Could smaller LM-templated nanozymes be produced (e.g., by adjusting
sonication conditions) to further improve tissue penetration?
2. Comparison to Other Approaches: The introduction could better distinguish this work from prior related studies. Although
the manuscript cites previous reports on LM-based nanozymes (Wu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), it does not sufficiently
articulate how the present study advances beyond these earlier efforts. It would be valuable for the authors to explicitly
highlight how their approach advances beyond previous reports, particularly in terms of the systematic composition tuning
and realization of a multi-enzyme cascade function with therapeutic efficacy. This clarification would better establish the
originality and significance of the current work.
3. Mechanistic Detail – Role of Indium vs Gallium: The study identifies an optimal Ga/In ratio; however, the mechanistic
reasoning for why both excessive and insufficient indium content are detrimental could be further elaborated. The authors
refer to prior work on charge distribution within Ga–In alloys (ref 67), indicating that indium incorporation increases structural
disorder and enhances electron density around gallium. They conclude that lower or higher indium levels compromise
catalytic activity. This is a key insight and perhaps a more comprehensive discussion here would strengthen the
understanding of how composition ties to structure and catalytic activity.
4. Undefined Terms and Abbreviations: Several key terms and abbreviations that are central to the manuscript are not
defined upon first use:
- POD-like activity: The manuscript repeatedly refers to "POD-like activity," but fails to define "POD."
- ABTS: Used as a substrate in peroxidase-mimicking activity assays but not defined.
- ROS: The term "ROS" is frequently used but never defined.
- NADH: Although common in biochemical studies, NADH is not defined.
- The MTT method is mentioned as the method for cytotoxicity evaluation, but the manuscript does not define MTT.
5. Missing Figure Legends in Fig. 4C and Fig. 4F: Figures 4C (DPBF assay for O₂•⁻ detection) and 4F (NADH oxidation
spectra) lack in-figure legends. The data series in the plots are not labeled. The authors should include proper legends
directly in the figure.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript outlined the synthesis, characterisation and application of novel amorphous liquid Ga/MoSx structures. The
authors show that these materials, coined as nanozymes, showcase some impressive catalytic activity, and can be used in
biological contexts where their redox activity may confer therapeutic effects (e.g. for tumour cells). Overall, I am highly
impressed by the work contained in this manuscript. I note that the uncovering of cascade catalysis that relies on the liquid
metal system is a particularly interesting finding. Therefore, I would consider the work of interest to the readership, and
of good quality for Nat. Commun. However, I believe there are several areas requiring clarification or amendment before I can
recommend the manuscript for publication.
Major comments:
1. The manuscript could benefit from clarifying the physical state of the LM/MoSx systems, especially during catalysis
testing. The LMs were presumably melted and in liquid form during synthesis of the LM/MoSx structures, but can they still be
considered to be in the liquid state during application? This is perhaps especially relevant in the biological context, where
temperature ranges are limited and must be carefully controlled.
2. The authors discuss the dynamic nature of liquid metals as key to enhancing their catalytic activity in the introduction, but
later suggest the activity of their LM/MoSx systems may be due to an abundance of active sites and interesting electronic
characters in the amorphous structure. Several groups are now releasing atomistic modelling suggesting that the dynamic
motion of liquid metal systems still plays a key role as well:
a. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56222-0
b. https://doi.org/10.1039/D3SC04416E
c. https://doi.org/10.1002/ange.202407124
The manuscript would benefit from addressing this discussion point in the context of their results. In particular, perhaps the
ongoing dynamics of a liquid metal based system may have links to true enzymatic character?
3. I strongly suggest the authors move the computational details of the density functional theory calculations to the main text
(i.e. in the methods). A reader should ideally be able to find the software used and exchange-correlation functional in the
main text.
4. More detail should be included on how the MoSx and LM/MoSx structural models were developed/selected for DFT. Did
the authors perform at-temperature molecular dynamics simulations? Were these structures adapted from other work? As is,
it is impossible to identify whether these models are representative or accurate for the system they are trying to describe. This is
especially true of the LM system, where a single snapshot is often not sufficient.
5. Can the authors clarify whether HSE06 was used for all DOS calculations as well as determination of the band centres?
Was it also used for the charge density analyses? This needs to be clearly stated in the methods or results.
6. It was unclear to me exactly which quantity is plotted in Figure 5A on the charge density analyses. Does this plot contain
the simple charge density obtained form the CHGCAR in VASP? Or is this a charge density difference relative to some
reference state (e.g. MoSx and LM separate)? I would suggest the later analysis is more meaningful for showing charge
accumulation (e.g. at Mo atoms, as the authors identify in the LM/MoSx system).
7. The DOS plots in 5B should likely be enlarged to make them more clear. It is difficult to read detailed information from
them.
8. The analysis of a d-band centre in Mo is interesting. I recommend the following paper for its interesting discussion on how
it is the gap between Mo and S states in MoS2 that determines redox activity for hydrogen evolution, rather than the d-band
centre: https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202003091. Could the authors comment on whether they think a similar analysis would
be of benefit here?
Minor corrections:
1. In the introduction the authors begin to use abbreviations without defining them in the text. (e.g. POD-like activities, LM,
OXD- and NOX-like are defined in the abstract but not the main text). These should be defined in their first mention in the
main text.
2. Should have "an" added in two places in the following sentence: "Here we design and screen the liquid metals-buffered
nanozymes, in which the liquid metals can not only initiate phase engineering to generate AN amorphous nanozyme with
abundant catalytic active sites, but also afford AN electron-rich microenvironment to optimize the electronic structure of
nanozymes for improving the catalytic performance (Fig. 1). "
3. "... free delocalized electrons cloud" should likely read "... free delocalized electron clouds"

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Next is the summarization of our point-by-point response to the comments raised by
the reviewers.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript reports the design of LM-buffered amorphous MoSx
nanozymes using Ga-In alloys as templates. The authors synthesize a series
of Ga1-x Inx MoSx nanozymes and identify Ga75.5 In24.5 MoSx as exhibiting
superior POD-like activity compared to crystalline MoS2. They attribute this
enhancement to LM’s roles in templating, inducing amorphization, and
providing an electron-rich microenvironment. The optimized nanozyme
demonstrates multi-enzyme activities (POD-, OXD-, and NOX-like), enabling
cascade reactions that disrupt redox/metabolic homeostasis in tumor cells. In
vitro and in vivo studies show efficient ROS generation, GSH/NADH depletion,
mitochondrial damage, and tumor growth inhibition. DFT calculations suggest
electron transfer from LM optimizes the electronic structure for catalysis. The
work applies established methodologies without demonstrating a significant
conceptual or practical leap beyond existing literature. The absence of
comparative analysis with relevant systems and recurring presentation issues
further diminishes its suitability for Nature Communications. Should the
authors address these gaps (e.g., by rigorously benchmarking against
competitors and clarifying the innovation boundary), this study may find a
better fit in a specialized journal. Therefore, I recommend rejection
in its current form.
Major Weaknesses Reinforcing Rejection:
1. Combines two well-explored materials (LM + MoS2) without novel design
principles or mechanistic insights. The concept of using LM (Ga-In alloys) for
catalysis is well-established (e.g., Refs 23–30, 62–63), as is MoS2-based
nanozyme design (Ref 55). The work combines these existing strategies
without introducing a transformative mechanism, material, or application.
Response: We are grateful for the time and effort the reviewer has spent in
reviewing our manuscript. The review comments are very helpful for further
strengthening the manuscript.
As for the previous works mentioned by the reviewer, references 23-30
focused on the catalytic performance of liquid metal on propane
dehydrogenation or electrocatalytic reaction. References 62 reported on
engineering liquid metal-based nanozyme for enhancing microwave dynamic
therapy, and their study focused on solving the problem of poor delivery of
microwave sensitizer and the obstacle of tumor hypoxic microenvironment in
microwave dynamic therapy (MDT). However, their nanozyme catalytic activity
was attributed to the Co2+ center in ZIF-67 rather than the liquid metal.
References 63 reported the galvanic replacement synthesis of
VOx@EGaIn−PEG for high-performance biosensors, and their study focused
on solving the limitations in biocompatibility, regenerability and recyclability of
b of
biosensors. References 55 reported that positive and negative charges,
produced on the surface of piezoelectric material under ultrasound (US), could
enhance the POD-like activity of MoS . These studies laid the key foundation
2
for our work, which revealed the great potential of liquid metal for nanozyme
catalysis. However, these studies are mainly focus on the various application
of LM-based catalysts, while overlooking the potential of liquid metal with
intrinsic amorphous property and unusual electronic microenvironment in
regulating nanozyme catalytic activity.
Our work highlighted the catalytic potential of liquid metals for screening and
regulation of nanozyme activity. We have not only investigated the catalytic
activity of liquid metal-buffered nanozyme with different gallium indium ratios,
but also explored the role of liquid metal in regulating catalytic performance
and the reasons for the enhanced enzyme-like catalytic activity of liquid
metal-buffered nanozyme. In particular, we have performed the density
functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the electronic structure of
LM-based nanozymes in the manuscript (Fig. 5). The calculation results
revealed that, compared to MoS , the LM MoS model not only achieved the
increased electron density of Mo, but also appeared a significantly higher DOS
near the Fermi level and several new hybrid electronic states. Moreover, the
LM MoS nanozymes exhibited an upward shift d band center position, which
X
was significantly nearer to the Fermi level than MoS . These changes
2
contributed to the electron transfer and the interaction between the adsorbed
substrate and LM MoS nanozyme, thereby favoring the catalytic reaction. In
X
addition, our designed LM-based nanozyme exhibited multienzyme mimetic
activity, i.e., POD-like activity, OXD-like activity, NOX-like activity, which could
work together to achieve multiple-enzyme-like cascade catalytic reactions to
disrupt intracellular redox and metabolic homeostasis. Our work provides not
only the first example of leveraging LM as a well-designed platform to screen
high-performance nanozyme with excellent therapeutic effects, but also
highlights the roles of tailored electronic structure and phase engineering for
regulation of catalytic activity of nanozymes.
In the revision, we have performed additional experiments and provided more
data to revise the manuscript, which further strengthens our catalyst design
and the understanding of the role of liquid metal in nanozyme catalysis.
Hopefully, it is more rigorous and integrated than the original version.
In the revised manuscript, we emphasized in the introduction section:
“However, the potential of liquid metal in regulating nanozyme catalytic activity
has rarely been explored mechanistically. In particular, previous research
efforts have focused on the application of liquid metal-based nanozyme while
overlooking the catalytic potential of liquid metals for screening and regulation

With regard to the tumor accumulation of nanoparticles, according to the
predominant belief in the nanotechnology community, nanoparticles cross the
tumor vascular barrier through intercellular gaps between adjacent endothelial
cells and are retained in the tumor owing to pressure created by poor
lymphatic drainage — a process termed ‘enhanced permeability and retention’
(EPR) (Nat. Rev. Mater. 2016, 1, 16014). For tumor blood vessels, adjacent
endothelial cells adhere to each other less tightly, forming interendothelial cell
gaps across the vessel wall. These gaps were found to have a size range up to
2,000 nm (Nat. Mater. 2020, 19, 566). Nanoparticles should be designed with
sizes smaller than the size of interendothelial gaps to accumulate inside the
tumor. Researchers have found that tumor vessels were permeable to
liposomes of up to 400 nm in actual diameter (Cancer Res. 1995, 55, 3752).
Moreover, Du’s research group have synthesized a cerium single-atom
nanozyme (Ce SAs@NC) with a hydrodynamic size of 370.2 nm (J. Am. Chem.
Soc. 2024, 146, 34092). Fluorescence images of mouse organs 24 h after
injection showed nanozyme accumulation in the liver and tumor. Ning’s
research group have constructed a dual-atom sites nanozyme (FeCu-DA), and
the hydrodynamic size was determined to be approximately 300 nm (Adv. Sci.
2025, 12, 2414734). They have investigated the biodistribution of FeCu-DA
nanozyme, and found that the fluorescence intensity was notably high in the
tumor, liver, and kidney, suggesting that nanozyme effectively accumulated in
tumor tissue and was primarily cleared through the hepatic and renal pathways.
Their data also confirmed that nanoparticles with a hydrodynamic size larger
than 300 nm exhibited selective uptake by tumor.
Moreover, the size measured by DLS is usually larger than the actual size of
nanoparticle observed under TEM. This discrepancy is likely caused by
variations in the degree of coating expansion, which can be attributed to the
relatively weak electrostatic interactions under different conditions (Angew.

With regard to the tumor accumulation of nanoparticles, according to the
predominant belief in the nanotechnology community, nanoparticles cross the
tumor vascular barrier through intercellular gaps between adjacent endothelial
cells and are retained in the tumor owing to pressure created by poor
lymphatic drainage — a process termed ‘enhanced permeability and retention’

endothelial cells adhere to each other less tightly, forming interendothelial cell
gaps across the vessel wall. These gaps were found to have a size range up to
2,000 nm (Nat. Mater. 2020, 19, 566). Nanoparticles should be designed with
sizes smaller than the size of interendothelial gaps to accumulate inside the

3. Mechanistic Detail – Role of Indium vs Gallium: The study identifies an
optimal Ga/In ratio; however, the mechanistic reasoning for why both
excessive and insufficient indium content are detrimental could be further
elaborated. The authors refer to prior work on charge distribution within Ga–In
alloys (ref 67), indicating that indium incorporation increases structural

understanding of how composition ties to structure and catalytic activity.
Response: Thanks for your professional suggestion. Yu and coworkers
investigated the effects of alloying Ga with In on the atomic structure and
electronic transport properties of liquid EGaIn using the AIMD simulations.
They found that with In alloying of Ga, their larger atomic volume leads to the
disordered structure as well as weak inter-atomic interactions by expanding
the cell volume and broadening their inter-atomic distance. Moreover, the
altered free-electron density is higher between Ga atoms, while the charge
density near the In atoms is significantly smaller. This feature of the In atoms
explain the dominant role of In in reducing the electrical transport property and
electrical conductivity (J. Chem. Phys. 2014, 140, 064303). As mentioned in
the introduction section, the catalytic active sites and local electronic
characteristics determine their catalytic performance to a large extent.
According to previous studies, the higher electrical conductivity favors efficient
electron transport, which is beneficial to improve the catalytic performance of
nanozyme (Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 5365; Adv. Mater. 2025, 37, 2502804).
Meanwhile, amorphous materials possess distinctive disordered atomic
arrangement that enables them with abundant active sites and optimized
electronic configurations, which are beneficial for enhancing their catalytic
properties (Nat. Commun. 2019, 10, 4855; Chem. Rev. 2023, 123, 13489).
Thereafter, we mentioned that “the alloying of Ga with In results in a more
disordered structure, and the charge density is higher between Ga atoms while
significantly smaller in the vicinity of In atoms” in the manuscript. To further
strengthen the understanding of composition and catalytic activity, we
supplemented that the Indium content in GaIn alloys significantly affects the
disordered structure and the charge density distribution of alloys, thus
influencing their amorphous structure and electrical conductivity. Specifically,
the alloying of Ga with In causes more disordered structure. This amorphous
structure is beneficial for the high catalytic performance of catalysts. However,
the electrical conductivity of GaIn alloys decreases with In alloying of Ga
because the charge density near the In atoms is significantly smaller, which is
unfavorable to the electron transfer and the subsequent catalytic process.
Thus, the catalytic activity of the resulting nanozymes could show a trend of
initially increasing and then decreasing with increasing In content in the GaIn
alloy. We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful and constructive
suggestion, and we have added the corresponding discussion into the revised
manuscript.

catalysts by providing a constantly evolving, self-healing, flexible, and highly
active interface, thus conferring optimal selectivity towards specific products at
the molecular level. These unique features encourage further exploration of
liquid metal catalysts for various other reactions.
As the reviewer pointed out, we have discussed in the introduction that the
liquid metal could create dynamic uniform catalytic sites and favorable
electronic structures for catalytic metal species, which remarkably enhanced
their catalytic capability (Nat. Chem. 2017, 9, 862; Nat. Chem. 2022, 14, 935;
Nat. Nanotechnol. 2024, 19, 306). These studies were similar to the
above-mentioned papers. Nevertheless, our current study was mainly focused
on leveraging the unusual electronic structure and phase engineering ability of
liquid metal to regulate nanozyme catalytic activity. Their liquid nature plays a
key role in the liquid-liquid interfacial reactions during the synthesis process
and is critical for the amorphous structure of the resulting nanozyme (Adv.
Mater. 2023, 35, e2303533; Chem. Soc. Rev. 2024, 53, 7158). After detailed
characterization and DFT calculations, the current experimental results
confirmed the unique role of liquid metals in nanozyme catalysis.
Moreover, in the above-mentioned literature, the catalytic active sites of
catalysts are atomically dispersed within the liquid metal, leading to a dynamic
coordination environment. However, in our work, the designed nanozyme are
more like a core-shell heterogeneous nanostructures. The MoS shell is
X
generated by using liquid metal as a template, which maintains the typical
amorphous characteristics of liquid metal. Meanwhile, the liquid metal within
the nanozyme affords an electron-rich microenvironment to optimize the
electronic structure of nanozymes. Based on their different microstructures,
the dynamic nature of liquid metals and their relevance to enzyme-like
characteristics should be carefully considered in the catalytic process of
nanozyme. To clarify this relevance, more complicated modeling and
calculations are needed. Dynamic sampling simulations of substrates and
catalysts are highly necessary. However, there are obstacles including the
multi-scale character of the processes, the spatial and chemical heterogeneity,
and the high-dimensional phase space, which are difficult for sufficient
statistical sampling. We thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive
suggestion, which is highly instructive. We will focus on the relationship
between the dynamic motion of liquid metal and the catalytic activity of
nanozymes in future work.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
After the revision, the quality of the manuscript has significantly improved, and it has largely resolved most of my concerns.
Several minors still need amendment.
1. Applying DLS and SEM measurements can only demonstrate the dimensional stability rather than the composition
stability. For instance, the low Mo leakage rate cannot guarantee the absence of LM-based phase separation. Therefore,
characterizations such as TEM or XPS are recommended to verify the stability of LM-based nanozymes.
2. The response to excellent tumor penetration of LM-MoSX nanozyme (ca. 300 nm) is not convincing. Referring to Fig. S38,
the fluorescence image showed that the LM-MoSX@Cy3 was located in the center of the liver rather than at the boundary
(what if Cy3 leakage occurs), so the 3D reconstruction image in IVIS should be provided. As Reviewer 3 suggested, an
investigation into the correlation between size and penetrability LM-MoSX nanozyme could help. Moreover, I wonder if other
imaging techniques (e.g., CT, MRI or PET) could be employed to trace the real-time and dynamic distributions of LM-MoSX
nanozyme.
3. I strongly agree with Reviewer 4 that whether the models used in theoretical calculations are representative or accurate
for LM-based nanoparticles, since they are hybrid nanomaterials (with varying and dynamic compositions) rather than
monodispersed nanomaterials reported previously, such as metal oxides and single-atom catalysts.

(2) As for the correlation between size and penetrability of nanoparticles, researchers
have investigated the accumulation and effectiveness of different sizes of
nanoparticles in tumors. For example, Yuan and coworkers found that tumor vessels
are less permselective than normal vessels, presumably due to large pores in the
vessel wall (Cancer Res. 1995, 55, 3752). They showed that tumor vessels were
permeable to liposomes of up to 400 nm in diameter, suggesting that the cutoff size of
the pores is between 400 and 600 nm in diameter. Bawendi and coworkers developed
a size series of luminescent, water-soluble particles within the 10-150 nm size range
for the purpose of studying the size-dependent properties of particle distributions in
solid tumors (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2010, 49: 8649-8652). They found that the 12 nm
nanoparticles extravasate easily, though heterogeneously, and diffuse away from the
vessels with minimal hindrance. In contrast, the 60 nm nanoparticles do extravasate
but do not leave the immediate perivascular space (they remain within 10 mm of the
vessel walls), whilst the 125 nm particles do not appreciably extravasate. Moreover,
Kataoka and coworkers have demonstrated that a variety of sub-100 nm polymer
micelles of different sizes (30 nm, 50 nm, 70 nm and 100 nm) penetrate well within
highly permeable tumors (Nat. Nanotechnol. 2011, 6, 815). However, in a poorly
permeable human pancreatic adenocarcinoma, characterized by low vascularity and
dense fibrosis, only small size nanoparticles <50 nm in diameter are able to
accumulate in tumors. The extent of nanoparticle accumulation also varies depending
on tumor type due to the interplay of various microenvironmental factors (Nat.
Biotechnol. 2015, 33, 941). In general, nanoparticles with large particle size tend to
have elevated blood circulation time and prefer to accumulate surrounding tumor
tissues through enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) phenomenon.
Comparatively, small-sized nanoparticles are more advantageous in penetrating into
deep tumor tissues, yet are frequently restricted by their rapid clearance from the body
and insufficient accumulation within tumor region (ACS Nano 2023, 17, 20825).
Apart from these, recent studies showed that nanoparticles enter the tumor through
active endothelial transport processes, are retained in the tumor due to interactions
with tumor components (Nat. Rev. Bioeng. 2024, 2, 201). Researchers found that
nanoparticles cross tumor endothelial cells predominantly using the
non-receptor-based macropinocytosis pathway. They discovered that tumor
endothelial cell membrane ruffles capture circulating nanoparticles, internalize them
in intracellular vesicles and release them into the tumor interstitium. Tumor
endothelial cells have a higher membrane ruffle density than healthy endothelium,
which may partially explain the elevated nanoparticle tumor accumulation. They
found the nanoparticle-releasing exocytosis pockets ranged from 89 nm to 841 nm in
diameter, suggesting that nanoparticles in this size range could accumulate more in
the tumor than in other non-MPS (mononuclear phagocytic system) organs through
this pathway. Moreover, this pathway has been verified in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice
(Nat. Nanotechnol. 2025, 20, 672). Therefore, we chose nanoparticles with relatively
smaller sizes to achieve better tumor therapeutic effect in our work.

Mater. 2023, 35, 2203391). Moreover, liquid metal exhibits the large absorption at

high-quality contrast agent for photoacoustic (PA) imaging (Adv. Mater. 2022, 34,
2201956; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 6779). For example, Liu and coworkers
reported that gallium microparticles are demonstrated to enhance the T2 magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) effect and mediate the dual-mode imaging of CT and MRI
(Adv. Funct. Mater. 2020, 30, 2003359). Miyako and coworkers reported liquid metal
nanocapsules could be used for photoacoustic and X-ray imaging (Nat Commun 2017,
8, 15432). In addition, Mo-based nanomaterials can be applied to contrast agents in
CT imaging because Mo atom with high absorption coefficient and atomic number
has stronger X-ray attenuation than the components of the body (ACS Nano 2014, 8, 7,
6922; Adv. Sci. 2021, 8, 2100165). Furthermore, molybdenum sulfide nanoparticles
have outstanding photothermal conversion efficiency and excellent NIR absorption

## Abstract

Liquid metals (LMs) have been used for design of advanced materials by leveraging their unique liquid and electronic properties. Here, we design a series of liquid metal-buffered amorphous molybdenum sulfide nanozymes with different gallium indium ratios, in which Ga In MoS 75.5 24.5 X nanozymes exhibit the enzyme-like activity, superior to the crystalline MoS . This has been verified and assigned to the roles of liquid metal: (i) serving as the building template, (ii) phase engineering with catalytic active sites, (iii) electron-rich microenvironment for improving catalytic activity. Besides, the amorphous Ga In MoS nanozyme possesses oxidase (OXD)-like and 75.5 24.5 X S nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide oxidase (NOX)-like activiSty to achieve multiple-enzyme-like E cascade catalytic reactions, disrupting intratumoral redox and metabolism homeostasis. As the R example of leveraging liquid metal as a well-desiPgned platform to screen high-performance N nanozyme with excellent therapeutic effects, thNis work highlights the roles of tailored electronic I structure and phase engineering for regula tion of catalytic activity of nanozymes and may also E broaden the application of liquid metaLl in catalysis and biomedical field.

---

## Introduction

Liquid metals (LMs) aAre enigmatic materials, with simultaneous metallic and liquid nature.1, 2 The most striking features of liquid metals are the amorphous property and unusual electronic microenvironment, which originate from the electron-rich metallic cores and free delocalized electron clouds.3, 4 Such characters make liquid metals show great potential to tune the physical, chemical, and electronic properties of materials for boosting their performance in various engineering applications.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 More importantly, liquid metals represent a promising technical route for manufacturing modular advanced materials.3, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 The obtained combinatorial materials can readily maintain the typical characteristics of liquid metals and may attain better functionality.20 In particular, the intrinsic amorphous nature of liquid metals creates a facile pathway for phase engineering of materials, thus deriving more intriguing properties and innovative applications.21, 22 Interestingly, liquid metals have also shown promising prospects in catalysis by capitalizing on their unique electronic properties.23, 24, 25, 26 For example, recent studies have reported that liquid metals could create dynamic uniform catalytic sites and favorable electronic structures for catalytic metal species to remarkably enhance their catalytic capability.27, 28, 29 Similarly, liquid metals have been proposed as a unique electron mediator for temporary electron storage, and promoted the extraction and transfer of electrons, as well as charge separation, greatly improving the optoelectronic property of perovskite films.30 Furthermore, the representative Ga-based liquid metal alloys with excellent biocompatibility and attractive flexibility, have recently aroused great interest in the biological field including cancer therapy, antimicrobial treatment, and bioimaging.31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, S39, 40, 41, 42, 43 These studies indicate the exceptional advantages of liquid metals to create advanced materials for catalytic and biomedicine applications.

Nanozymes are nanomaterials with inherent Nenzyme-mimicking catalytic properties, and have ignited increasing attention due to their adv antages of high catalytic stability and durability, easy preparation, and low cost.44, 45, 46, 47 ALlthough promising, the unsatisfactory catalytic efficiency of nanozymes remains a crucial issue for future practical applications.48, 49, 50, 51, 52 This demonstrates the vital necessity of developing an appropriate strategy to optimize the nanozyme catalytic performance. From aAn in-depth perspective, the catalytic active sites and local electronic characteristics determine their catalytic performance to a large extent.49, 50, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57 Notably, phase engineering of nanomaterials has demonstrated remarkable prospects in the catalysis field because this process modulates the atomic arrangements and electronic structure of catalysts, hence providing unusual catalytic activity.58, 59 Especially, amorphous materials possess distinctive disordered atomic arrangement that enables them with abundant active sites and optimized electronic configurations, which are beneficial for enhancing their catalytic properties.60, 61 Thus, combining the ability of phase engineering and the unique electronic properties, liquid metals are expected to be a dream matrix to construct high-performance nanozymes. However, the potential of liquid metal in regulating nanozyme catalytic activity has rarely been explored mechanistically. In particular, previous research efforts have focused on the application of liquid metal-based nanozyme while overlooking the catalytic potential of liquid metals for screening and regulation of nanozyme activity. 62, 63

Here we design and screen the liquid metals-buffered nanozymes, in which the liquid metals can not only initiate phase engineering to generate an amorphous nanozyme with abundant catalytic active sites, but also afford an electron-rich microenvironment to optimize the electronic structure of nanozymes for improving the catalytic performance (Fig. 1). We first prepare a series of molybdenum sulfide nanozymes by using five liquid metals with the composition of Ga In 1-x x (with x=0, 0.125, 0.245, 0.375, and 0.50) as templates, and these nanozymes feature uniformly core-shell structure and amorphous property. We observe that tShese nanozymes exhibit peroxidase (POD)-like activities, in which the LM MoS nanozymes (LM=Ga In ) present the best X R 75.5 24.5 catalytic activity. Then, the role of liquid metals inP regulating the enzyme-mimicking catalytic activity of LM MoS nanozymes is explored. WNe demonstrate that, compared to crystalline MoS , X 2 the amorphous LM MoS X nanozymes expo se abundant active sites and defects, and show about a 10-fold increase in the POD-like catalLytic activity, together with a significantly higher glutathione (GSH) consumption ability. Meanwhile, this strategy can turn on the oxidase (OXD)-like and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide oxidase (NOX)-like activities of LM MoS to achieve cascade X catalytic reactions, eveAntually leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrate that the LM MoS nanozymes with multienzyme-mimicking X catalytic activity can trigger a highly efficient cascade reaction to disrupt intratumoral redox and metabolic homeostasis, eventually killing tumor cells. In this work, we introduce liquid metal with advantages in synthesis and catalysis to screen and regulate the catalytic and therapeutic effects of nanozymes for efficient tumor inhibition. Our work not only investigates the catalytic activity of liquid metal-buffered nanozyme with different gallium indium ratios, but also elucidates the mechanism underlying the enhanced enzyme-like catalytic activity through density functional theory (DFT) calculations. This study offers promising insights into the design and regulation of nanozymes, with potential benefits for future biomedical applications of liquid metals.

## Results

The design and preparation of liquid metal-buffered nanozymes
As shown in Fig. 1a, the nanozyme was synthesized through facile probe sonication. Liquid metals with different ratios of gallium and indium were prepared by dissolving a calculated amount of In pellets in liquid Ga. The resultant liquid metal alloys should retain their liquid states at close to room temperature to ensure the subsequent liquid-liquid interfacial reactions.64 According to the previous reports, the molar fraction of In should below 50 at% in order to ensure their liquid states at close to room temperature.65, 66 Specifically, the composition of Ga In (with x = 0, 0.125, 0.245, S1-x x 0.375, and 0.50) were chosen and prepared to design a series oSf liquid metal-buffered nanozymes. Molybdenum is a low-cost and biocompatible transition metal with multiple oxidation states, which endows Mo-based nanomaterials with tunablPe enzyme-like activity.67 Among Mo-based nanomaterials, molybdenum sulfide features unNique structural and electronic properties and show superior performance in various applica tions, especially for catalysis.68, 69 The generated nanozymes were denoted as Ga 50 In 5L0 MoS X , Ga 62.5 In 37.5 MoS X , Ga 75.5 In 24.5 MoS X , Ga 87.5 In 12.5 MoS , Ga MoS . During this procedure, liquid metal served as a template to trigger in situ X 100 X galvanic replacement reactions between liquid metal droplets and MoS 2- ions to produce core– 4 shell nanostructures uApon ultrasonication. The thermodynamic driving force underlying the galvanic replacement reaction originates from the difference in redox potentials between the two metal-based species.21, 64 The size distribution of nanoparticles became narrower with higher sonication intensity applied (Supplementary Fig. 1). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images illustrated the well-constructed core-shell structures of the synthesized five nanozymes (Fig. 2a). Then, the energy dispersive spectroscopic (EDS) mapping and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results demonstrated the existence of Ga, In, Mo and S elements in these nanozymes (Supplementary Fig. 2-3). Next, high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) images indicated the amorphous nature of five nanozymes (Fig. 2a). According to previous studies, the intrinsic amorphous nature of liquid metals and short reaction time are considered the main reasons for the formation of the amorphous structure.4, 11 Dynamic light scattering (DLS) results of five nanozymes revealed that their hydrodynamic diameters were mainly distributed around 300 nm (Fig. 2b). The surface zeta potential measurement showed that these nanozymes were negatively charged (Fig. 2c). Then, we explored the POD-like activity of five nanozymes by monitoring the oxidation of 2, 2'-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS) at 415 nm. As revealed in Fig. 2d and 2e, obvious ABTS oxidation could be detected, indicating that all five nanozymes possessed POD-like activity. Among them, Ga In MoS exhibited the highest 75.5 24.5 X catalytic activity, while Ga In MoS showed a relatively low activity. According to previous 50 50 X studies, the Indium content in GaIn alloys significantly affects the disordered structure and the charge density distribution of alloys, thus influencing their aSmorphous structure and electrical conductivity.70 Specifically, the alloying of Ga with In causes more disordered structure. This amorphous structure is beneficial for the high catalPytic performance of catalysts. However, the electrical conductivity of GaIn alloys decreasesN with In alloying of Ga because the charge density I near the In atoms is significantly smaller, which is unfavorable to the electron transfer and the E subsequent catalytic process of catalyLsts. Thus, the catalytic activity of the resulting nanozymes C could show a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing with increasing In content in the I T GaIn alloy. These findings could explain the experimental results that the alloying effect of In with R Ga favored the catalyAtic reaction, while lower or higher In contents compromised the catalytic activity. We further employed XPS spectra to characterize the electronic properties of these nanozymes. ### Reviewer 1

This manuscript reports the design of LM-buffered amorphous MoSx nanozymes using Ga-In alloys as templates. The
authors synthesize a series of Ga1-x Inx MoSx nanozymes and identify Ga75.5 In24.5 MoSx as exhibiting superior POD-like
activity compared to crystalline MoS2. They attribute this enhancement to LM’s roles in templating, inducing amorphization,
and providing an electron-rich microenvironment. The optimized nanozyme demonstrates multi-enzyme activities (POD-,
OXD-, and NOX-like), enabling cascade reactions that disrupt redox/metabolic homeostasis in tumor cells. In vitro and in
vivo studies show efficient ROS generation, GSH/NADH depletion, mitochondrial damage, and tumor growth inhibition. DFT
calculations suggest electron transfer from LM optimizes the electronic structure for catalysis. The work applies established
methodologies without demonstrating a significant conceptual or practical leap beyond existing literature. The absence of
comparative analysis with relevant systems and recurring presentation issues further diminishes its suitability for Nature
Communications. Should the authors address these gaps (e.g., by rigorously benchmarking against competitors and
clarifying the innovation boundary), this study may find a better fit in a specialized journal. Therefore, I recommend rejection
in its current form.
Major Weaknesses Reinforcing Rejection:
1. Combines two well-explored materials (LM + MoS2) without novel design principles or mechanistic insights. The concept
of using LM (Ga-In alloys) for catalysis is well-established (e.g., Refs 23–30, 62–63), as is MoS2-based nanozyme design
(Ref 55). The work combines these existing strategies without introducing a transformative mechanism, material, or
application.
2. Claims of LM’s unique roles lack substantial evidence, except for citing prior literatures
3. Catalytic performance lacks comparison to state-of-the-art LM-based catalysts or high-activity MoS2-based nanozymes.
Assertions of "superior activity" remain unsupported without context.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, Zhang et al. designed a series of liquid metal-buffered nanozymes and screened the most favorable
nanozyme to achieve efficient tumor catalytic therapy. The findings highlight the roles of tailored electronic structure and
phase engineering for regulating the catalytic activity of nanozymes. Authors demonstrate that this is the first report of
screening and regulating the catalytic and therapeutic effects of LM nanozymes to achieve efficient tumor therapy. The
overall work is well-designed, and the application of LM in catalysis and the biomedical field is interesting. However, at the
current stage, the characterization of the structure-activity relationship and the anti-cancer mechanism of LM-based
nanozyme is not solid. Also, other issues need to be addressed.
1)The most significant concern of utilizing LM-based nanozymes for catalytic cancer therapy lies in the intrinsic property of
LM. As is known, amorphous LM nanoparticles could gradually transform into crystalline material, especially in aqueous
solution. Due to such a dynamic process, the composition of LM-based nanozyme could hardly be maintained during in vitro
and in vivo experiments or characterizations. Also, it is necessary to ensure that the MoSx content in a series of LM-buffered
nanozymes is the same. Or else, the differences in nanozyme activity could also be influenced by different MoSx contents.
2)In a recently published paper (Small 2025, 2502752), FeOx was used to hybridize LM to generate nanozymes. Therefore,
the reason for choosing molybdenum sulfide should be clarified to distinguish the innovation of this work from previous
works, and the advantages of molybdenum sulfide should be explained as well.
3)It was demonstrated that Ga75.5In24.5 (commercial Gallium-Indium eutectic) MoSX performed the best catalytic activity,
but the possible reason was not given. With subtle variations of the compositions, the melting points and the fluidities of
resultant LM-MoSX nanozymes would alter significantly. In this context, the discussion of the catalytic activity of LM-MoSX
nanozymes should be careful. Additionally, the authors did not provide detailed synthesis methods and characterization
techniques. It is suggested to supplement relevant details.
4)Although decorating with HA, it remains challenging for LM-MoSX nanozyme (ca. 300 nm) to achieve efficient cellular
uptake and high accumulation in the stiff 4T1 tumor via intravenous injection (Figure S35). And what is the half-life of LM-
MoSX nanozyme?
5)In Figure S2B, D, the In 3d curves were poorly fitted.
6)In Figure S20, the curve shape of EPR result of O2•− seems abnormal. Please confirm the result and the discussion.
7)In Figure S27, why did the cellular fluorescence of DAPI present large deviations at variable time points?
8)The changes in particle size and potential of LM MoSx should be measured after the modification of HA.
9)In Figure S33, there is a difference in H&E staining of the lung between the H-LM MoSx group and the control group. Were
the images captured at the same magnification?
10)In Figure S35, quantitative data on in vivo biodistribution should be supplemented.
11)The stability test of the LM MoSx nanozymes should be provided.
12)In the article, POD-like activity was used to screen for suitable ratios of GaIn. Why not use other nanozyme activities for
screening?
13)In Figure 6J, the live and dead cells co-staining was not well performed, and the cell morphology could hardly be
distinguished.Please provide fluorescence images under high magnification.
14)The grammar and language of the manuscript should be carefully polished.

### Reviewer 3

The authors present a comprehensive and well-executed study on liquid metal-buffered MoSₓ nanozymes, systematically
synthesized using Ga–In alloys to optimize catalytic performance. The Ga₇₅.₅In₂₄.₅-based nanozyme exhibits enhanced
peroxidase-, oxidase-, and NADH oxidase-like activities, enabling a catalytic cascade that disrupts redox homeostasis in
cancer cells and induces selective cytotoxicity both in vitro and in vivo. The combination of multi-enzyme functionality,
effective tumor targeting, and minimal toxicity underscores the therapeutic potential of this platform. The study’s originality
lies in leveraging liquid metal templating to precisely control nanozyme composition, structure, and electronic properties,
representing a clear advancement over previous LM-based nanozyme approaches. The conclusions are well-supported by
comprehensive materials characterization, catalytic assays, theoretical modeling, and biological validation. The
experimental methodology is appropriate and rigorously executed. Overall, this work constitutes a significant contribution to
nanozyme research and catalytic cancer therapy.
To further enhance the manuscript, several clarifications and suggestions are
proposed as detailed in the following comments (also provided in the attached file).
1. Particle Size and Delivery: A potential concern is the relatively large hydrodynamic size of the nanozyme (~300 nm
diameter). Particles of this size may have limited tumor penetration and faster clearance by the mononuclear
phagocyte system. The in vivo success after HA coating suggests good tumor accumulation capability, but the authors might comment
on how the size could influence distribution. Could smaller LM-templated nanozymes be produced (e.g., by adjusting
sonication conditions) to further improve tissue penetration?
2. Comparison to Other Approaches: The introduction could better distinguish this work from prior related studies. Although
the manuscript cites previous reports on LM-based nanozymes (Wu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), it does not sufficiently
articulate how the present study advances beyond these earlier efforts. It would be valuable for the authors to explicitly
highlight how their approach advances beyond previous reports, particularly in terms of the systematic composition tuning
and realization of a multi-enzyme cascade function with therapeutic efficacy. This clarification would better establish the
originality and significance of the current work.
3. Mechanistic Detail – Role of Indium vs Gallium: The study identifies an optimal Ga/In ratio; however, the mechanistic
reasoning for why both excessive and insufficient indium content are detrimental could be further elaborated. The authors
refer to prior work on charge distribution within Ga–In alloys (ref 67), indicating that indium incorporation increases structural
disorder and enhances electron density around gallium. They conclude that lower or higher indium levels compromise
catalytic activity. This is a key insight and perhaps a more comprehensive discussion here would strengthen the
understanding of how composition ties to structure and catalytic activity.
4. Undefined Terms and Abbreviations: Several key terms and abbreviations that are central to the manuscript are not
defined upon first use:
- POD-like activity: The manuscript repeatedly refers to "POD-like activity," but fails to define "POD."
- ABTS: Used as a substrate in peroxidase-mimicking activity assays but not defined.
- ROS: The term "ROS" is frequently used but never defined.
- NADH: Although common in biochemical studies, NADH is not defined.
- The MTT method is mentioned as the method for cytotoxicity evaluation, but the manuscript does not define MTT.
5. Missing Figure Legends in Fig. 4C and Fig. 4F: Figures 4C (DPBF assay for O₂•⁻ detection) and 4F (NADH oxidation
spectra) lack in-figure legends. The data series in the plots are not labeled. The authors should include proper legends
directly in the figure.

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript outlined the synthesis, characterisation and application of novel amorphous liquid Ga/MoSx structures. The
authors show that these materials, coined as nanozymes, showcase some impressive catalytic activity, and can be used in
biological contexts where their redox activity may confer therapeutic effects (e.g. for tumour cells). Overall, I am highly
impressed by the work contained in this manuscript. I note that the uncovering of cascade catalysis that relies on the liquid
metal system is a particularly interesting finding. Therefore, I would consider the work of interest to the readership, and
of good quality for Nat. Commun. However, I believe there are several areas requiring clarification or amendment before I can
recommend the manuscript for publication.
Major comments:
1. The manuscript could benefit from clarifying the physical state of the LM/MoSx systems, especially during catalysis
testing. The LMs were presumably melted and in liquid form during synthesis of the LM/MoSx structures, but can they still be
considered to be in the liquid state during application? This is perhaps especially relevant in the biological context, where
temperature ranges are limited and must be carefully controlled.
2. The authors discuss the dynamic nature of liquid metals as key to enhancing their catalytic activity in the introduction, but
later suggest the activity of their LM/MoSx systems may be due to an abundance of active sites and interesting electronic
characters in the amorphous structure. Several groups are now releasing atomistic modelling suggesting that the dynamic
motion of liquid metal systems still plays a key role as well:
a. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56222-0
b. https://doi.org/10.1039/D3SC04416E
c. https://doi.org/10.1002/ange.202407124
The manuscript would benefit from addressing this discussion point in the context of their results. In particular, perhaps the
ongoing dynamics of a liquid metal based system may have links to true enzymatic character?
3. I strongly suggest the authors move the computational details of the density functional theory calculations to the main text
(i.e. in the methods). A reader should ideally be able to find the software used and exchange-correlation functional in the
main text.
4. More detail should be included on how the MoSx and LM/MoSx structural models were developed/selected for DFT. Did
the authors perform at-temperature molecular dynamics simulations? Were these structures adapted from other work? As is,
it is impossible to identify whether these models are representative or accurate for the system they are trying to describe. This is
especially true of the LM system, where a single snapshot is often not sufficient.
5. Can the authors clarify whether HSE06 was used for all DOS calculations as well as determination of the band centres?
Was it also used for the charge density analyses? This needs to be clearly stated in the methods or results.
6. It was unclear to me exactly which quantity is plotted in Figure 5A on the charge density analyses. Does this plot contain
the simple charge density obtained form the CHGCAR in VASP? Or is this a charge density difference relative to some
reference state (e.g. MoSx and LM separate)? I would suggest the later analysis is more meaningful for showing charge
accumulation (e.g. at Mo atoms, as the authors identify in the LM/MoSx system).
7. The DOS plots in 5B should likely be enlarged to make them more clear. It is difficult to read detailed information from
them.
8. The analysis of a d-band centre in Mo is interesting. I recommend the following paper for its interesting discussion on how
it is the gap between Mo and S states in MoS2 that determines redox activity for hydrogen evolution, rather than the d-band
centre: https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202003091. Could the authors comment on whether they think a similar analysis would
be of benefit here?
Minor corrections:
1. In the introduction the authors begin to use abbreviations without defining them in the text. (e.g. POD-like activities, LM,
OXD- and NOX-like are defined in the abstract but not the main text). These should be defined in their first mention in the
main text.
2. Should have "an" added in two places in the following sentence: "Here we design and screen the liquid metals-buffered
nanozymes, in which the liquid metals can not only initiate phase engineering to generate AN amorphous nanozyme with
abundant catalytic active sites, but also afford AN electron-rich microenvironment to optimize the electronic structure of
nanozymes for improving the catalytic performance (Fig. 1). "
3. "... free delocalized electrons cloud" should likely read "... free delocalized electron clouds"

Liquid metals (LMs) have been used for design of advanced materials by leveraging their unique liquid and electronic properties. Here, we design a series of liquid metal-buffered amorphous molybdenum sulfide nanozymes with different gallium indium ratios, in which Ga In MoS 75.5 24.5 X nanozymes exhibit the enzyme-like activity, superior to the crystalline MoS . This has been verified and assigned to the roles of liquid metal: (i) serving as the building template, (ii) phase engineering with catalytic active sites, (iii) electron-rich microenvironment for improving catalytic activity. Besides, the amorphous Ga In MoS nanozyme possesses oxidase (OXD)-like and 75.5 24.5 X S nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide oxidase (NOX)-like activiSty to achieve multiple-enzyme-like E cascade catalytic reactions, disrupting intratumoral redox and metabolism homeostasis. As the R example of leveraging liquid metal as a well-desiPgned platform to screen high-performance N nanozyme with excellent therapeutic effects, thNis work highlights the roles of tailored electronic I structure and phase engineering for regula tion of catalytic activity of nanozymes and may also E broaden the application of liquid metaLl in catalysis and biomedical field.
